extracted.intended_audience: scholars, policymakers, IP managers, and patent strategists interested in when patents capture innovation rents
extracted.subtask_description: Use the Cohen-Nelson-Walsh (CNW) framework to assess whether a given patent functions as an effective appropriability mechanism for the firm that holds it. The rubric emphasizes industry context, innovation type, strategic motives, claim-to-product mapping, disclosure tradeoffs, and complementary assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry reliance on patents as primary appropriability mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the firm's industry typically ranks patents as a primary way of protecting innovation rents (CNW: patents are dominant in pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and some chemicals; less so in most other industries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use industry norms from CNW and corroborating surveys: pharmaceuticals/biotech → patents primary; discrete mechanical industries → important but not always dominant; complex-product industries (semiconductors, software) → mainly defensive; process innovations → secrecy preferred. If an industry generally does not rely on patents, a patent for that industry is less likely to function as high-quality appropriability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic patenting motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the firm's motive(s) for patenting: prevention of copying; patent blocking; use in cross-licensing; prevention of suits; reputation/financing signaling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the stated or inferred motive aligns with claim scope and filing strategy. Motives that match claim drafting (e.g., blocking patents with broad families to prevent competitor filings) suggest coherent strategy; motives that are purely signaling or opportunistic may indicate lower appropriability value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation type matches patent strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the innovation is a product versus a process, and whether it is a discrete invention or part of a complex product; product and discrete inventions are better matched to patent protection than processes or complex-product innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product innovations (e.g., pharma compounds, mechanical parts) are more often effectively protected by patents. Process innovations often rely on secrecy; complex products (semiconductors, software) typically use patents defensively. A mismatch (e.g., trying to rely on patents for a process that is easier kept secret) is a signal of weaker patent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure does not defeat secrecy value
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether filing the patent (and thereby disclosing the invention) undermines the trade-secret protection that would otherwise preserve firm rents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent disclosure reveals knowledge that can be readily reverse-engineered or exploited by competitors, the patent may reduce rather than enhance appropriability. Patent quality in this dimension requires that disclosure captures genuinely novel, non-obvious information not easily reverse-engineered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of lead time and complementary assets
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the firm's lead time advantages and complementary assets (manufacturing scale, distribution, brand) align with the patent's role (defensive vs offensive) and whether the patent covers the firm's actual products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality patents in this sense: cover actual products (not aspirational), have clear scopes amenable to licensing or cross-licensing, and are positioned defensively or offensively in a way consistent with the firm's broader IP strategy. If lead time or complementary assets dominate capture of rents, patents may be secondary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims map onto products the firm sells or expects to sell
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether patent claims are written to cover the firm's own commercial products or planned offerings rather than only broad external possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that closely map to the firm's commercial output indicate coherent appropriability use—facilitating enforcement and licensing. Claims that do not relate to the firm's product portfolio may signal nuisance, blocking-only, or rent-seeking patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation strategy preserves options for capturing competitor designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the firm uses continuation/divisional filings strategically to maintain flexibility in claim scope as competitor designs evolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A continuation strategy that preserves later claim amendments can be a marker of strategic, high-quality patenting (allowing capture of emergent competitor designs). Lack of such a strategy may reduce the patent family's strategic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-license potential recognized in claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether patents are drafted with potential cross-licensing value in mind (e.g., claiming technologies likely to be complementary or contested in negotiations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents intended as cross-license currency should have claims that intersect with competitors' technologies and are clear enough to be bargained over. If claim drafting ignores cross-license opportunities, the patent's strategic exchange value is reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-markers of low-quality or nuisance strategic patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify red flags: claims drafted to capture only competitor products (not the firm's own), no connection between patents and the firm's R&D investments, and acquired portfolios used solely for assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of these anti-markers suggests patents are nuisance, troll-like, or principally for assertion rather than coherent appropriability; such patents may satisfy formal patentability but have low economic appropriability value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmaceutical / biotechnology-specific quality criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: In pharma/biotech, patents are primary appropriability mechanisms; quality requires structural specificity, robust claim layering, and defenses against generics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate patent quality for structural specificity (precise molecular/structural claims), claim layering (families and continuations creating multiple claim scopes), and legal/market defenses (regulatory exclusivities, formulation/usage claims) to deter generics. In this industry, patent quality heavily determines commercial value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrete mechanical industries criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: In discrete mechanical industries patents are important; quality requires clear scope and resistance to design-arounds, though lead time and brand often matter more than mere claim breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claims are drafted to resist simple design-arounds and whether the patent complements lead-time and branding advantages. Broad but vague claims may be less valuable than narrowly tailored, design-around-resistant claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex-product industries criteria (semiconductors, software)
rubrics_metrics.description: In complex-product industries patents tend to be defensive (cross-license currency); quality emphasizes standard-essential or design-essential coverage and scope clarity over breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality patents in these industries often claim features that are essential to design or standards, or otherwise are clear and enforceable in cross-licensing contexts. Vague, overly broad patents are less useful when products are complex and modular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process innovation criteria (secrecy vs patent trade-offs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For process innovations, patents are weaker appropriability tools; patent quality requires that the disclosure be tolerable given the trade-secret alternative, and patents are typically filed when reverse engineering is feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the process can be protected better as a trade secret. If disclosure via patent materially lowers the firm's rents (e.g., makes the process easy to replicate), then the patent is lower-quality as an appropriability mechanism. Patents for processes make more sense when reverse engineering would reveal the process anyway.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNW Quality Test (synthesis of evaluative questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise checklist: Does the firm's industry rely on patents as a primary appropriability mechanism? Does the patent cover the firm's actual or planned commercial products? Is the strategic motive consistent with claim drafting? Does the disclosure preserve trade-secret value where applicable? Does the patent fit the firm's broader IP/competitive strategy?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist as a quick, synthesized test of appropriability coherence. A patent that answers these questions positively is deemed higher-quality in the CNW framework even if it merely meets formal patentability standards.
